title: Why doesn't the Moon fall to Earth?
subtitle: Orbit & gravity
subject: sciences
description: The Moon is constantly falling toward Earth. She just misses it every time. That's exactly what an orbit is.

hero.hook: The Moon is falling towards us. She just misses Earth every turn.

blocks.text: If Earth's gravity pulls the Moon, why doesn't it crash into us? The answer seems bizarre: the Moon **is indeed falling** towards the Earth. She just misses it every moment.

This balance between fall and lateral speed is a **orbital**, a curved trajectory around a star. The English physicist **Isaac Newton** was the first to unify the fall of an apple and the movement of the stars with the same idea.
If you weighed **60 kg** on Earth, you would only weigh about **10** on the Moon: its gravity is six times weaker.
Newton imagines a cannon on top of a mountain so high that it would emerge from the atmosphere. We shoot a ball horizontally. With little power, it falls quickly. With more force, he goes further.

blocks.caption: Newton's cannonball thought experiment: the key to understanding orbit.

blocks.text: At a specific speed, called , something remarkable happens. As the ball falls, the Earth, which is round, curves under it at the same rate. The projectile falls… without ever touching the ground. He is in **permanent free fall**, pulled by gravity without crashing. [[Satellite speed]]
The Moon does the same thing. She has enough side speed to turn a fall into a loop. Without this speed, it would dive straight towards us.

The Moon orbits at approximately **384,000 km**. Its lateral velocity is approximately **1 km/s**. If it stopped suddenly, it would crash within days. If gravity suddenly disappeared, it would go in a straight line in space, according to the principle of : a body maintains its speed if it is not slowed down. [[Inertia]]

says that every mass attracts every other mass, and that the attraction decreases with distance, more precisely with the square of the distance. The closer a satellite is, the faster it must go to avoid falling. [[Newton's universal gravitation]]
The International Space Station, at just **400 km** altitude, is traveling at around **28,000 km/h**. It goes around the Earth in **90 minutes**. The Moon, further away, takes **27.3 days**.
So the orbit is not magic. It's a constant compromise between "I'm falling" and "I'm moving too fast to hit."

The orbit is not fixed. The s come into play. The Moon's gravity pulls harder on the side of the Earth facing it than on the center. It deforms the oceans and creates a bulge of water. [[Tidal forces]]

As the Earth rotates on its axis faster than the Moon rotates around it, this ridge advances a little in front of the Moon. Friction slows the Earth's rotation very slightly: our days lengthen by approximately **1.4 milliseconds** per century. In exchange, the Moon moves away by about **3.8 cm** per year.

Billions of years ago, the Moon was much closer. The tides were huge. This mixing of water and chemistry may have helped early life forms. And the dinosaurs lived on an Earth where the days only lasted **22 or 23 hours**.

Today, by geometric coincidence, the Sun is about **400 times** larger than the Moon, but also **400 times** farther away. The two therefore have the same **apparent size**, the angle at which we see them in the sky. Total solar eclipses are possible.

In about **600 million years**, the Moon will be too far away to completely obscure the Sun. All that will remain are annular eclipses: a ring of light around the lunar disk. In the very long term, the Earth and the Moon could synchronize: each body would always show the same face to the other. But the Sun, by becoming **red giant**, final phase of a star like ours, will transform the system much earlier.
The Moon does not crash because its lateral speed balances the Earth's attraction: it is in permanent free fall. And it is still moving away by about **3.8 cm** per year.
